narrative:
The model estimated a 96.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first try. In practical terms, the admissions decision treated that as a very high risk of not meeting the school’s bar-passage expectation, so your application was denied.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile—roughly the lowest group—while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap was the single most influential factor and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the next most important factor; you were also in the first decile there, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, and it also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor: 27 versus an accepted-student average of about 37. That difference also increased the predicted risk of bar failure. Together, these academic indicators outweighed other details in your profile. Your gender and race were not used to make this prediction.

To move forward, ask admissions whether a review or feedback session is available, and clarify any application errors. If you reapply, focus on the areas that drove this decision: prepare for and consider retaking the LSAT, strengthen your academic record through additional coursework if feasible, and seek schools or programs that consider a broader range of evidence. Also ask for specific bar-readiness supports and document any improvement before reapplying.
